title: How do you implement pagination and sorting in JPA using setFirstResult/setMaxResults and Spring Data's Pageable and Sort?
shortTitle: Pagination and sorting with Pageable and Sort?

s1_definition.profdef: At the JPA level, `query.setFirstResult(offset)` and `query.setMaxResults(limit)` paginate a result set. Spring Data abstracts this with `Pageable` (page number, page size, and sort) and `Sort`; repository methods accepting a `Pageable` return a `Page` (with total count) or a `Slice` (without a count query). Sorting is expressed via `Sort.by(...)` and translated into an ORDER BY clause.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of Rajesh asking for his transaction history "20 at a time, newest first." setFirstResult is "skip the first N," setMaxResults is "give me 20." Spring Data's Pageable is a tidy request form that bundles "page 3, 20 per page, sorted by date descending" into one object, and Page is the reply that also tells you "there are 4,000 total." Slice is the lighter reply that just says "here are 20, and yes there is more" without counting everything.
s1_definition.oneliner: setFirstResult/setMaxResults are the raw JPA knobs; Pageable/Sort/Page wrap them cleanly, with Page adding a total count and Slice skipping it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** At the JPA level, `query.setFirstResult(offset)` and `query.setMaxResults(limit)` paginate a result set. Spring Data abstracts this with `Pageable` (page number, page size, and sort) and `Sort`; repository methods accepting a `Pageable` return a `Page` (with total count) or a `Slice` (without a count query). Sorting is expressed via `Sort.by(...)` and translated into an ORDER BY clause.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of Rajesh asking for his transaction history "20 at a time, newest first." setFirstResult is "skip the first N," setMaxResults is "give me 20." Spring Data's Pageable is a tidy request form that bundles "page 3, 20 per page, sorted by date descending" into one object, and Page is the reply that also tells you "there are 4,000 total." Slice is the lighter reply that just says "here are 20, and yes there is more" without counting everything.

**One line to remember:** setFirstResult/setMaxResults are the raw JPA knobs; Pageable/Sort/Page wrap them cleanly, with Page adding a total count and Slice skipping it.

sections.s2_technical:
Raw JPA: `em.createQuery("select t from Txn t order by t.createdAt desc", Txn.class).setFirstResult(40).setMaxResults(20).getResultList()` returns rows 41–60. setFirstResult is zero-based offset; setMaxResults is the page size. These map to SQL LIMIT/OFFSET.

Spring Data Pageable: a repository method `Page<Txn> findByAccountId(String id, Pageable p)` accepts `PageRequest.of(2, 20, Sort.by(Sort.Direction.DESC, "createdAt"))` meaning page index 2 (the third page), 20 per page, sorted by createdAt descending. Spring runs the data query AND a separate `count` query so the returned `Page` knows total elements and total pages.

Page versus Slice: `Page` triggers an extra COUNT(*) which can be expensive on large tables. `Slice` skips the count — it fetches size+1 rows internally to know if there is a next page, which is cheaper and ideal for infinite scroll where you do not need a total.

Sort: `Sort.by("balance").descending().and(Sort.by("id").ascending())` builds multi-column ordering. You can pass Sort alone (without pagination) to a method returning a List for a fully sorted result. Always include a unique tiebreaker like id so ordering is deterministic when the primary sort has ties.

Senior nuances: sorting on an unindexed column forces a filesort and can be slow; add an index matching the ORDER BY. The COUNT query in Page can dominate cost on huge tables, so prefer Slice or keyset pagination there. Also, pagination with JOIN FETCH on a collection is problematic because the join multiplies rows and the in-memory pagination warning appears — paginate the root entity, then fetch collections separately.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh wants his mini-statement 20 transactions at a time, newest first. This is exactly Pageable with a page size and a descending sort on the date.

Problem 2 — The operations dashboard needs to show "page 3 of 200" with a total count. This is exactly a Page result, which runs a count query.

Problem 3 — The mobile app does infinite scroll and does not need a total. This is exactly a Slice, which skips the count for speed.

Problem 4 — A report sorts accounts by balance descending, then by id for stable ordering. This is multi-column Sort.

We will build a StatementService returning Page, Slice, and sorted lists.

```bash
# Run
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh SAV2001, page index 2, size 20, newest first.

Step 1 — The service builds a PageRequest for page 2, size 20, sorted by createdAt descending with id as a tiebreaker.

Step 2 — For the Page call, Spring runs the data query `... WHERE account_id=? ORDER BY created_at DESC, id ASC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40` returning rows 41–60, and a second query `SELECT count(*) WHERE account_id=?` so the Page reports totalElements and totalPages.

Step 3 — For the Slice call, Spring runs only the data query but fetches 21 rows (size+1); if 21 come back it knows hasNext is true and returns the first 20. No COUNT runs, so it is faster.

Step 4 — For the sorted account report, `findAll(Sort.by("balance").descending().and(Sort.by("id")))` produces `ORDER BY balance DESC, id ASC`, giving a deterministic order even when two accounts share a balance.

```
Hibernate: select ... where account_id=? order by created_at desc, id asc limit ? offset ?
Hibernate: select count(t.id) from txns t where account_id=?
INFO  Page 2/200 total=4000
Hibernate: select ... order by created_at desc limit ?   (size+1, no count)
INFO  Slice page 2 hasNext=true
```

```
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<interface>> TxnRepository │

  │  + ...OrderByCreatedAtDesc    │ returns Slice
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Cost model ──
  Page  → data query + COUNT(*)  (count can dominate on huge tables)
  Slice → data query (size+1)     (cheaper, no total)
  Sort on unindexed col → filesort (slow); index matching ORDER BY → fast

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. page(SAV2001,2,20) → PageRequest(2,20,DESC)
  2.   data query LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40
  3.   count query → totalElements
  4. return Page(content, totals)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
At the raw JPA level, pagination is just two methods: setFirstResult sets the zero-based offset and setMaxResults sets the page size, which translate to LIMIT and OFFSET in SQL. Spring Data wraps this much more cleanly with a Pageable object that bundles the page number, page size, and sort direction, so a repository method accepting a Pageable can return a Page or a Slice. Sorting is expressed with Sort.by and becomes an ORDER BY clause, and I can compose multiple columns and directions.

The distinction I always call out is Page versus Slice. A Page runs a second count query so it can report the total number of elements and pages, which is exactly what a dashboard needs to render "page 3 of 200." A Slice deliberately skips that count and instead fetches one extra row to know whether a next page exists, which makes it cheaper and ideal for infinite scroll where the user never needs a grand total. On very large tables the count query behind a Page can dominate the cost, so I switch to Slice or keyset pagination there.

In our National Bank of India system, Rajesh's mobile mini-statement uses a Slice sorted by date descending because the app only needs twenty transactions and a "load more," while the operations dashboard uses a Page because it must show totals. A report that ranks accounts by balance uses a multi-column Sort with a unique tiebreaker on the id so the ordering is deterministic even when two accounts share the same balance.

The senior details I add are that sorting on an unindexed column forces a filesort and can be slow, so I add an index that matches the order-by clause, and that paginating a query which join-fetches a collection is dangerous because the join multiplies rows and Hibernate falls back to in-memory pagination. In that case I paginate the root entity first and fetch its collections separately, or I use keyset pagination for deep scrolling where offset-based paging would degrade.

---

keyPoints: Return type: Page<T> (with total count) or Slice<T> (without count)
Slice is faster — skips COUNT(*) query
